newsitem.title: UAE: Iran holds regional conference on Afghanistan.
newsitem.headline: Iran holds regional conference on Afghanistan.

text.p: Iran on Tuesday opened a regional conference in Tehran to seek a solution to the Afghan crisis, but Pakistan, a key player in neighbouring Afghanistan, stayed away from the talks.

State-run Tehran radio said Foreign Minister Ali Akbar Velayati opened the two-day conference, attended by delegates from the United Nations, Russia, China, India, Turkey, the Organisation of the Islamic Conference as well as Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan.
Journalists in Tehran said Velayati told a news conference that Ireland sent an official to represent the European Union.
Although invited to the conference, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Uzbekistan did not send delegates.

"It is hoped that this regional conference could lay the ground for a healthy international conference with the aim of bringing peace, tranquility and reconstruction to this brotherly and neighbourly country," Velayati said in his opening speech.
He said any lasting solution to the war in Afghanistan "should come through the participation of all political and ethnic groups in an inter-Afghani dialogue".

Velayati said the United Nations had not done enough to draw world attention to the plight of Afghanistan's people and urged the world body to stop the intervention of "foreign countries in Afghanistan's internal affairs".

He was apparently referring to Pakistan, which the Iranian media have accused of setting up the Sunni Moslem Taleban with backing from the U.S. and funding from Saudi Arabia to counter Iran's influence in the region.
Pakistan, which plays an active role in Afghanistan, denies the charge and says it has no favourites among Afghan factions.
Pakistan said on Sunday it would not attend the conference citing problems with the agenda and guest list, which includes arch-foe India.

Velayati later told the news conference that Iran understood Pakistan's "important role" in Afghanistan and expressed hope that "in the future we will have Pakistan's contribution to regional cooperation".

Pakistan and Iran have been working closely together in diplomatic moves over Afghanistan during 17 years of civil war there, but differences appeared between them after the emergence of the Taleban as a new factor in Afghan politics.
Velayati reiterated that Iran, which last week branded Taleban as "rebels", recongnised the government of ousted President Barhanuddin Rabbani.
The official Iranian news agency IRNA on Monday said U.N. envoy Francis Okelo told Velayati the conference "was a fundamental step towards universal efforts for returning peace to Afghanistan".

Okelo was sent to Iran by U.N. special envoy to Afghansitan Norbert Holl, who has been trying to broker a ceasefire between the Islamic Taleban movement and its foes after the Taleban forced out the government from Kabul in September.
Velayati warned at the conference that if the fighting does not stop by the winter the world should expect to face "a more serious human tragedy in Afghanistan".
